title: The schools of thought in macroeconomic analysis
competency: Describe and compare the classical, neoclassical, Keynesian, monetarist, new classical and new Keynesian schools of thought.

en.text: The classical view, from Adam Smith to Irving Fisher, dominated until the Great Depression: with flexible prices the economy returns quickly to full employment, so policy should be "hands off"; fiscal expansion only crowds out private investment and monetary expansion only raises prices. Supply-siders such as Arthur Laffer stress the harm of taxes; the Laffer curve shows that cutting tax rates can sometimes raise revenue. Neoclassical economics (Walras, Marshall, Pareto) adds marginal utility and mathematics and holds that, in the long run, flexible wages and prices return the economy to potential GDP.

screens.title: The Laffer curve
screens.ask: The tax base shrinks as the rate rises: base = 1,000 × (1 − rate). Move the tax rate. Where is revenue largest?
screens.note: Revenue is 0 at a 0 % rate and at 100 %. A tax cut raises revenue only above the peak (here 50 %).

Neoclassical suits the long run; Keynesian suits the short run.

en.text: The Great Depression of the early 1930s showed that markets did not correct themselves and contradicted Say's law, "supply creates its own demand". John Maynard Keynes argued that real GDP depends on aggregate demand, which is unstable; recessions happen because demand can be too low for full employment and because wages and prices are sticky. Keynesians see monetary policy as weak in a depression and prescribe active fiscal policy — more government spending — to raise demand, employment and output.

Fiscal policy works: more government spending raises demand, employment and output.

en.text: Milton Friedman and the monetarists argued that monetary policy, not fiscal policy, addresses macroeconomic problems. Because investment is very sensitive to interest rates, fiscal policy strongly crowds out private investment and cannot change output or employment. Monetary policy has real effects, but long and variable lags make its timing risky and can worsen the business cycle, so Friedman proposed a constant growth rule for the money supply.

ideas.name: New classical and new Keynesian economics

en.text: New classical economists (Lucas, Sargent, Barro, Prescott) are modern classicals: they use mathematics and assume flexible prices and wages, rational expectations and efficient markets, so fluctuations are rational responses to incentives; their policy ineffectiveness proposition says policy makers cannot or should not use countercyclical policy. New Keynesians (Akerlof, Phelps, Taylor, Fischer, Blanchard, Mankiw), writing in the 1970s and 1980s, accept rational expectations but stress nominal rigidities from multi-period wage contracts, so stabilisation policy can work; recent work stresses imperfect competition, coordination failures and credit limits.

screens.title: Can people be fooled?
screens.ask: The government announces it will print much more money next month. People expect higher prices and raise their wages and prices now. What happens to output?
opts: Little or nothing: mainly prices rise
screens.after: If people expect the policy and adjust at once, it may change only prices. This is the new classical idea behind the "policy ineffectiveness proposition".

screens.title: New classical economics
paras: The natural successors of the classical economists.
Robert Lucas, Thomas Sargent, Robert Barro, Edward Prescott.
They stress mathematical techniques.
Flexible prices and wages, rational expectations, efficient markets, full employment.
Fluctuations are rational responses to incentives, not nominal rigidities.
Policy ineffectiveness proposition: policy makers cannot or should not use countercyclical policy.

screens.title: New Keynesian economics
paras: The natural successors of the Keynesians, writing in the 1970s and 1980s.
George Akerlof, Edmund Phelps, John B. Taylor, Stanley Fischer, Olivier Blanchard, Gregory Mankiw.
Markets may not be as perfect as classical economists suggest.
They accept rational expectations, but stress nominal rigidities from multi-period wage contracts.
So the policy ineffectiveness proposition fails; policy can stabilise the economy.
Recent work is more micro-based: imperfect competition, coordination failures, credit restrictions.

notes.text: p.18: the classical paragraph says fiscal expansion "would only cause inflation", then that it fully crowds out investment "without effecting changes in the price level" ("effecting" → "affecting"). The lesson teaches: fiscal expansion → full crowding out; monetary expansion → only higher prices.
p.19: misplaced comma in the neoclassical building blocks. They are (1) potential GDP determines the size of the economy, and (2) wages and prices adjust flexibly.

p.21: life dates are out of date — Edward Prescott died in 2022 and Robert Lucas in 2023. Other "(year –)" dates should be checked; the lesson omits dates of living economists. "So are the new Keynesians" should read "… the natural successors of the Keynesians".
The Laffer slider and calculation, the delayed-steering hook, the 4 % money-growth example and the schools comparison table (from Activity 1.3) are added.
